name: Constant-step BDF2 ODE integration
definition: For y′=f(t,y) and t_n=t_0+nh with constant h>0, solve (3y_(n+1)−4y_n+y_(n−1))/(2h)=f(t_(n+1),y_(n+1)) for n≥1. For y′=λy, with z=hλ, the characteristic equation is (3−2z)r²−4r+1=0.
variables: h positive constant step; t_n grid time; y_n state; f right-hand side; λ scalar test rate; r characteristic root
assumptions: Smooth initial-value problem with a locally Lipschitz right-hand side, bounded solution derivatives through order three, O(h²) accurate starting states and sufficiently accurate implicit solves on a fixed finite interval
limitations: Constant-step coefficients are not valid on arbitrary unequal grids; startup and implicit solves are required; second-order convergence and scalar linear stability do not imply accuracy for large steps or unconditional nonlinear solvability
failure_conditions: Unresolved implicit solve, nonfinite state or unacceptable scaled residual
Missing starting state or changed step spacing without a different validated formula
computation: Supply y_0 and y_1 on the same grid, for example obtain y_1 using one converged backward Euler step from exact y_0, whose local state error is O(h²) under smoothness assumptions. Solve residual R(v)=3v−4y_n+y_(n−1)−2h f(t_(n+1),v)=0 on the locally consistent solution branch, using a declared finite solve budget and scaled tolerance; for smooth convergence analysis require state-equation solve errors O(h³) per step or smaller. Reject unresolved or nonfinite solves; a small residual alone is not a global error certificate.

source.citation: Sun, L. (2016), Analysis of backward differentiation formula for nonlinear differential-algebraic equations with 2 delays, SpringerPlus 5, 1013, Eq. (18) for the ordinary differential equation, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40064-016-2422-z ; truncation and characteristic roots independently derived for the constant-step ODE only.

required_inputs: ODE, initial values or starting procedure, constant step and solve budget
mechanism_note: A two-step implicit backward derivative approximation with history and a distinct characteristic polynomial, rather than one-step backward Euler or endpoint quadrature. Zero-step-rate roots are 1 and 1/3. Taylor expansion at t_(n+1) gives a derivative defect of O(h²).

name: Implicit midpoint ODE integration
definition: For y′=f(t,y), solve y_(n+1)=y_n+h f(t_n+h/2,(y_n+y_(n+1))/2). For y′=λy, z=hλ gives amplification R(z)=(1+z/2)/(1−z/2).
variables: h positive step; t_n time; y_n state; f right-hand side; λ scalar test rate; z scaled rate
assumptions: Smooth right-hand side and solution with bounded derivatives through the order required for second-order convergence, locally Lipschitz dynamics and sufficiently accurate implicit solves on a fixed finite interval
limitations: Not L-stable since R(z) tends to −1 for large negative real z; scalar linear A-stability does not guarantee nonlinear solvability, physical invariants for arbitrary systems or accuracy at large steps
failure_conditions: Unresolved midpoint stage, unacceptable scaled residual or nonfinite state
Failure to select the locally consistent implicit solution
computation: For each step solve K=f(t_n+h/2,y_n+hK/2), then set y_(n+1)=y_n+hK. Use a declared finite solve budget, scaled residual tolerance and locally consistent root; require state-update error O(h³) per step or smaller for second-order convergence analysis. Reject unresolved solves. A step refinement comparison is an indicator, not a certified error bound.

source.citation: LeMesurier, B., Introduction to Numerical Methods and Analysis with Julia (draft), §7.3, implicit midpoint equation and implicit trapezoid comparison, https://lemesurierb.people.charleston.edu/introduction-to-numerical-methods-and-analysis-julia/docs/ODE-IVP-2-Runge-Kutta.html ; order and scalar amplification independently derived. Idaho National Laboratory TMAP8 search result was not used as a verified source because the linked page returned 404.

required_inputs: ODE right-hand side, initial state, step and nonlinear solve policy
mechanism_note: One-stage implicit Runge–Kutta evaluates the vector field at the midpoint of time and state. It is generally different from averaging endpoint vector fields in trapezoidal integration, although the scalar autonomous linear amplification is identical. Distinct implicit stage mechanism from the existing explicit RK4 and RK23.
